questions.q: Why is storing a cloud storage key as a Kubernetes Secret considered risky compared to Workload Identity or IRSA?
options: Secrets cannot be mounted into Pods at all
Secrets are visible in plain text to every user in the cluster by default
It's a long-lived credential that must be rotated manually and remains valid until someone notices a leak and revokes it
Kubernetes does not support Secrets larger than 1KB
questions.explain: A stored key is durable and must be manually rotated; if it leaks, it stays valid until someone catches it. Federated identity avoids storing any such key.

questions.q: What does Azure Workload Identity actually federate?
options: A Kubernetes ServiceAccount with an Azure AD (Entra ID) application, using the ServiceAccount's own token as proof of identity
A Kubernetes Namespace with an Azure resource group
A Kubernetes Secret with an Azure Key Vault secret
An entire AKS cluster with a single Azure subscription
questions.explain: Workload Identity ties a specific ServiceAccount (namespace + name) to an Azure AD application via a federated credential, with the ServiceAccount's token itself used to prove identity — no client secret stored.

questions.q: What does `eksctl create iamserviceaccount --attach-policy-arn ... --approve` accomplish in one command?
options: It creates an EC2 instance profile instead of an IAM role
It grants the ServiceAccount full AdministratorAccess regardless of the policy specified
It creates the IAM role, trusts it to the cluster's OIDC provider, and annotates the ServiceAccount so Pods using it get scoped temporary AWS credentials
It only creates a Kubernetes ServiceAccount object with no AWS-side configuration
questions.explain: This single eksctl command handles IAM role creation, OIDC trust configuration, and ServiceAccount annotation together — this is IRSA (IAM Roles for Service Accounts).

questions.q: How does `az aks update --attach-acr` let node pools pull private container images without imagePullSecrets?
options: It requires every Pod to mount a Secret regardless
It grants the AKS node pool's managed identity pull access directly to Azure Container Registry
It disables image pull authentication entirely for the cluster
It copies the registry's admin password into every Pod spec
questions.explain: Attaching ACR to the node pool's managed identity lets nodes authenticate to the registry directly, removing the need for per-Pod imagePullSecrets.

questions.q: What is the common thread between AKS Workload Identity and EKS IRSA?
options: Both only work for pulling container images, not for accessing other cloud resources
Both require storing a long-lived API key in a Kubernetes Secret
Both are exclusive to EKS and were later ported to AKS
Both let a Kubernetes ServiceAccount obtain short-lived, automatically issued cloud credentials via an OIDC trust relationship, with no durable secret stored
questions.explain: Despite different names and cloud-specific mechanics, both features federate a Kubernetes ServiceAccount's identity into the cloud provider via OIDC, issuing short-lived credentials instead of relying on a stored key.
